items_per_order.note: Poisson rejected due to heavy mass at k=1 (90%). Empirical weights [p1,p2,p3+] used in locustfile.

status_ratios.pending_explanation: PENDING is written to orders_db at SAGA Step 1 then immediately overwritten to CONFIRMED or FAILED within the same synchronous HTTP request. GET /orders/{id} called after POST /orders returns will always see CONFIRMED or FAILED. Fold 0.3% PENDING into CONFIRMED/FAILED when computing locustfile expected outcome ratios.

orders_per_user_distribution.scale_up_assumption_vs_olist: Olist real e-commerce data exhibits extreme single-purchase churn (96.88% one-time buyers, mean 1.035 orders/user). In enterprise distributed OMS load-testing, virtual users must exercise user order history pagination (GET /orders?user_id) and recommendation traversal on recurring baskets, requiring an operational target mean of ~40 orders/user across 1.25M users. An unconstrained Pareto model caused pathological concentration where a single user accumulated 524,617 orders (52.5% of volume). Replacing Pareto with a truncated lognormal (mu=1.0, sigma=1.7, cap=2000) preserves a heavy-tailed customer repeat profile (small median=9, p90=86, p99=503) scaled up by an effective factor of 3.445x, while capping the top 1% volume at 23.69%.

arrival_rate.shape: use real Olist hourly/weekday profiles unchanged
arrival_rate.level: scale lambda by 531.3x - multiply each time-slot weight by target lambda
arrival_rate.example: peak-hour rate uses hourly_profile weights from fit_report.json scaled to target lambda=47.5282 orders/min

viva_explanations.1_order_value_log_normal: Order values follow a log-normal distribution. That means if you take the natural log of each order total, the resulting values are bell-shaped (normal). This is the standard model for revenues and prices because prices are multiplicative: a 10% discount on a $100 item moves it to $90, not $90±$10. The KS test p-value may be small (reject at α=0.05) because the right tail of real revenue data is slightly heavier than a true log-normal — this is normal for e-commerce and does not invalidate the model for simulation purposes.
viva_explanations.2_items_per_order_poisson: The number of distinct product lines per order was compared against a shifted-Poisson model (shifted because the minimum is 1, not 0). The model is rejected by chi-square because 90% of orders have exactly 1 item — a much sharper mass at 1 than Poisson predicts. In practice we use the empirical probabilities directly: P(1 item)=90%, P(2)=7.6%, P(3+)=2.3%. This is more honest and produces realistic load patterns.
viva_explanations.3_qty_per_line_geometric: Quantity per line item (how many units of one product per order) was compared against a Geometric distribution, which is the discrete analogue of the Exponential and models 'number of tries until success'. It's rejected for the same reason as items per order — 93% of lines have quantity 1. We use empirical weights: P(qty=1)=93%, P(qty=2)=5.3%, P(qty≥3)=1.7%.
viva_explanations.4_product_popularity_zipf: Product popularity follows Zipf's law (also called a power law): the most popular product is ordered roughly twice as often as the second most popular, three times more than the third, and so on. This is fitted by log-log linear regression — plotting log(rank) vs log(frequency) gives a straight line with slope ≈ -0.84. R²=0.957 means the line explains 95.7% of the variance in log-frequency. The same pattern appears in web traffic, word frequency in language (Zipf's original observation), and citation counts.
viva_explanations.5_arrival_rate_nonhomogeneous_poisson: Order arrivals are modelled as a Non-Homogeneous Poisson Process (NHPP). In a standard Poisson process the rate λ is constant. NHPP allows λ to vary with time. We extract two multiplier profiles from the real data: (a) hourly profile — how much of daily traffic falls in each of the 24 hours (peaks in the afternoon/evening), and (b) weekday profile — how traffic distributes across Monday–Sunday. A chi-square test against a flat (uniform) distribution rejects uniformity with p≈0, confirming the time-varying pattern. Under load testing these profiles can be used to modulate the Locust spawn rate.
viva_explanations.6_status_ratios_and_pending: The order-service SAGA (saga.py) writes status='PENDING' to the database at Step 1, then immediately overwrites it to 'CONFIRMED' (success) or 'FAILED' (compensation complete) within the same synchronous HTTP request. There is no async gap. So any GET /orders/{id} called after POST /orders returns will see CONFIRMED or FAILED — never PENDING in steady state. The 0.3% Olist 'PENDING' rows (status='created'/'processing') represent orders that were interrupted mid-flight (network crash, server restart) — not a normal operating mode. We fold that 0.3% proportionally: final ratios are CONFIRMED≈98.8%, FAILED≈1.2%.
viva_explanations.7_two_stage_category_product: A single global Zipf ranking across all 33 products conflicts with the real category share data. If we rank Electronics products 1-6 and Accessories 25-33, Zipf gives Electronics ~52% of picks but the real share is only 17.9%. Two-stage sampling fixes this: first draw a category with probability equal to its real Olist sales share (Electronics 17.9%, Accessories 28.3%, …), then within that category rank the local products 1..n and apply Zipf weights. This preserves both the power-law within-category skew and the correct cross-category proportions.
viva_explanations.8_scale_up_50M: Scaling from 99k Olist orders to 50M synthetic orders requires two adjustments: (1) Arrival rate: multiply the real lambda (0.089 orders/min) by the scale factor (~535x) to reach ~47.5 orders/min. The empirical hourly and weekday profiles stay intact; only the volume level scales. (2) Orders per user: Olist has a mean of 1.03 orders per user (97% one-time buyers). At 50M orders over 1.25M users the mean must be 40. Pure Pareto with alpha=1.026 is mathematically flawed for synthesis because its unbounded variance allowed a single user to monopolize 52% of all orders. We replaced Pareto with a Truncated Lognormal model (mu=1.0, sigma=1.7, hard cap=2000). The unconstrained lognormal mean is exp(1.0 + 1.7^2/2) = 11.53, and clipping to [1, 2000] yields mean 11.61. Normalized probability weights are scaled by N/U = 40 (an effective scaling factor of 3.445x). The real 50M database yields: mean=39.99, median=9.0, p90=86, p99=503, max=2,000, with the top 1% users owning 23.69% of volume (KS stat = 0.287).
